notes.text: The angel of God — Whose ministry was made use of in the pillar of cloud and fire, went from before the camp of Israel, where they did not now need a guide; there was no danger of missing their way through the sea, and came behind them, where now they needed a guard, the Egyptians being just ready to seize the hindmost of them. There it was of use to the Israelites, not only to protect them, but to light them through the sea; and at the same time it confounded the Egyptians, so that they lost sight of their prey, just when they were ready to lay hands on it. The word and providence of God have a black and dark side towards sin and sinners, but a bright and pleasant side towards those that are Israelites indeed.

We have here the history of that work of wonder which is so often mentioned both in the Old and New Testament. An instance of God's almighty power in dividing the sea, and opening a passage through the waters. It was a bay, or gulf, or arm of the sea, two or three leagues over. The God of nature has not tied himself to its laws, but when he pleases dispenseth with them, and then the fire doth not burn, nor the water flow. They went through the sea to the opposite shore; they walked upon dry land in the midst of the sea; and the pillar of cloud being their rereward, the waters were a wall to them on their right hand, and on their left. Moses and Aaron it is likely ventured first, into this untrodden path, and then all Israel after them; and this march through the paths of the great waters would make their march afterwards through the wilderness less formidable. This march through the sea was in the night, and not a moon-shine night, for it was seven days after the full moon, so that they had no light but what they had from the pillar of fire. This made it the more awful, but where God leads us, he will light us; while we follow his conduct we shall not want his comforts.

And the Egyptians went in after them into the midst of the sea — They thought, why might they not venture where Israel did? They were more advantageously provided with chariots and horses, while the Israelites were on foot.

The Lord — Called the angel before, looked - With indignation, upon the Egyptians, and troubled the Egyptians - With terrible winds and lightnings and thunders, chap. xv, 10, Psalm lxxvii, 18, 19. Also with terror of mind.

They had driven furiously, but now they drove heavily, and found themselves embarrassed at every step; the way grew deep, their hearts grew sad, their wheels dropt off, and the axle-trees failed. They had been flying upon the back of Israel as the hawk upon the dove; but now they cried, Let us flee from the face of Israel.

And the Lord said unto Moses, Stretch out thy hand over the sea — And give a signal to the waters to close again, as before upon the word of command they had opened to the right and the left. He did so, and immediately the waters returned to their place, and overwhelmed all the host of the Egyptians. Pharaoh and his servants, that had hardened one another in sin, now fell together, and not one escaped. An ancient tradition saith, That Pharaoh's magicians Jannes and Jambres perished with the rest. Now God got him honour upon Pharaoh, a rebel to God, and a slave to his own barbarous passions; perfectly lost to humanity, virtue, and all true honour; here be lies buried in the deep, a perpetual monument of divine justice: here he went down to the pit, though he was the terror of the mighty in the land of the living.
After them — That is, after the Israelites.

And Israel saw the Egyptians dead upon the shore — The Egyptians were very curious in preserving the bodies of their great men, but here the utmost contempt is poured upon all the grandees of Egypt; see how they lie heaps upon heaps, as dung upon the face of the earth.

And Israel feared the Lord, and believed the Lord and his servant Moses — Now they were ashamed of their distrusts and murmurings; and in the mind they were in, they would never again despair of help from heaven; no not in the greatest straits! They would never again quarrel with Moses; nor talk of returning to Egypt. How well were it for us, if we were, always in as good a frame, as we are in sometimes! In this chapter, I. Israel looks back upon Egypt with a song of praise for their deliverance. Here is,

glossa.text: *And the angel of God lifting himself up,* etc. ((STRAB.)) The angel, who is interpreted *messenger,* signifies the teachers, who announce to us the precepts of life, and with the cloud, that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures, go before the camp of Israel, that is, the Church, because with the knowledge of the Scriptures they preside. When the Egyptians come upon them he goes back behind, because in the time of persecution they set themselves in front on behalf of their subjects. But the cloud was dark to the Egyptians, bright to the Hebrews.

*All the night,* etc. Because through the whole time of this life, which the night signifies, the grace of the Holy Spirit makes the waters of baptism passable to the faithful, that they may pass over from spiritual Egypt into the land of promise: but it chokes the army of the enemy.

((ISID.)) The Red Sea signifies the baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ; the enemies following at the back die together with their king, because past sins are blotted out in baptism, and the devil is choked: the Egyptians press on as far as the sea, and sins as far as baptism. After the passage of the Red Sea the people sing, the enemies being drowned; and the faithful, coming up from the laver, their sins extinguished, chant a hymn, saying: *Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously,* etc.

notes.text: Judah — Or Israel, one tribe being put for all. Judah he mentions as the chief of all the tribes.
The mountains — Horeb and Sinai, two tops of one mountain, and other neighbouring mountains.

Tremble — The mountains did more than what was fit at the appearance of the great God. We are to give glory to God, not to ourselves or idols, ver. 1-8. By trusting in his promise and blessing, ver. 9-15. And by praising him, ver. 16-18.

glossa.text:
*At the going out.* ((AUG.)) Here things past are not related, but things to come are foretold, because in those deeds things to come were signified: and therefore not all the things which were done there are spoken of here, but certain of them otherwise, lest he be thought to be recounting things past. ((CASS.)) First the Prophet tells what wonders God gave to the Hebrews in figure, and to Christians in spirit. Secondly he asks why these things were done, there, *What ailed thee, O sea?* Thirdly he reproves the empty idols of the Gentiles, and commends the religion of God, there, *the idols of the Gentiles.*

*At the going out.* As it were, when Israel, that is, the house of Jacob, went out of Egypt, that is, from a barbarous people.

 *Barbarous.* ((AUG.)) That tongue is barbarous which praises not God.
*It was made.* ((CASS.)) As that people, when it went out of Egypt, etc., *as far as* they are able to resist vices, and this.

*The sea saw,* that is, the sinners of the world. *Jordan,* they who by divers desires snatch men into the great sea, that is, into the embittering malice of this world; but these things cease at the coming of the Lord, being as it were turned backward.

*The sea saw.* ((AUG.)) This is here said otherwise than it was done. There it is read to have stood on that side from which the waters were flowing down, nor is anything said there of the mountains skipping; but both the things done there and the things said here are figures.

*Rams.* ((ID.)) Who with the horns of both, etc., *as far as* every knowledge lifting itself up against Christ. *The hills.* ((CASS.)) From tilling, the middling sort: for these things are not according to the letter; whence also by the sea and by Jordan, that is, by the ancient deeds, doubt not that those things are signified which today are done spiritually.
*What ailed thee.* ((ID.)) Secondly he asks why these things were, that he may stir up wonder. And he resolves it: *At the face of the Lord.*

*At the face.* ((ID.)) One answer for two, because one author both made the ages to be astonished, and made his own, that is, the mountains and the hills, to rejoice: for at the appearing of Christ men were moved from their own superstition to the worship of God.

*At the face of the God of Jacob.* And as though one should ask, who is the Lord? The God of Jacob, not a new one; who makes them wrestle.

*Who turned the rock.* ((ID.)) The hard hearts of the Jews, unto the water of baptism.

*The crag.* The Gentiles, that they also may pour forth the watering fountains of preaching.

((AUG.)) That is, himself, hard before, while he was not known, etc., *as far as* he might overflow upon all that believe, saying: *If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.*
*The house of Israel.* ((CASS.)) Here he shows the profit of the Christian religion.
*The house of Aaron.* ((AUG.)) But lest that should seem to be already a thing possessed by the greater which to the lesser is a hope, he adds, *The house of Aaron.*
*Mindful.* ((CASS.)) That he might convert them, and he blessed the converted through the same.

*Upon you.* ((AUG.)) Because the number of teachers increased.

*Upon the children.* Because the number of followers also increased. Therefore ye both, fathers and sons, are blessed of the Lord, who made you *heaven* in the greater, *and earth* in the lesser; or who made every creature.

*Blessed be ye of the Lord.* ((CASS.)) He who above wished to be blessed, now with confidence says, *Blessed,* which belongs to God, that ye may serve him. Truly *of the Lord,* because even *the heaven of heaven,* that is, Christ, is unto the honour of the Lord; or,

*The heaven of heaven,* that is, the empyrean, he gave to the Lord Christ, according as he is man. *But the earth.* This lower earth he gave. *To the children of men.* That in it they may purify themselves; or the people to the preachers; whence: As the Father hath sent me, and I will send you ((Joan. VI)).

*The heaven of heaven.* ((AUG.)) He speaks of those whose minds, etc., *as far as* whom the weak cannot yet see without a support.
*Nor all they that go down.* ((CASS.)) Or, not all they that go down; because the saints also went down, but not into the lower place.

notes.text: Him that is weak — Through needless scruples. Receive - With all love and courtesy into Christian fellowship. But not to doubtful disputations - About questionable points.
All things — All sorts of food, though forbidden by the law.

Despise him that eateth not — As over-scrupulous or superstitious. Judge him that eateth - As profane, or taking undue liberties. For God hath received him - Into the number of his children, notwithstanding this.
One day above another — As new moons, and other Jewish festivals. Let every man be fully persuaded - That a thing is lawful, before he does it.

Regardeth it to the Lord — That is, out of a principle of conscience toward God. To the Lord he doth not regard it - He also acts from a principle of conscience. He that eateth not - Flesh. Giveth God thanks - For his herbs.
None of us — Christians, in the things we do. Liveth to himself - Is at his own disposal; doeth his own will.
Or why dost thou despise thy brother — Hitherto the apostle as addressed the weak brother: now he speaks to the stronger.

As I live — An oath proper to him, because he only possesseth life infinite and independent. It is Christ who is here termed both Lord and God; as it is he to whom we live, and to whom we die. Every tongue shall confess to God - Shall own him as their rightful Lord; which shall then only be accomplished in its full extent. The Lord grant we may find mercy in that day; and may it also be imparted to those who have differed from us! yea, to those who have censured and condemned us for things which we have done from a desire to please him, or refused to do from a fear of offending him. Isaiah xlv, 23

glossa.text: *Now him that is weak.* It belongs to a perfect faith to distinguish no food, nor to think it unclean, because *all things are clean to the clean.* But certain weak ones judged that some things were to be abstained from, and so there was contention among the Romans; whence he enjoins that such be taken up, not cast off, but by bearing with them, by example and by word, to be raised up to faith. And if it is unknown with what mind anyone does a thing, not to dispute about it. *Not in disputes.* He is not to be condemned whose thought is not open, or of whom we know not what sort he will afterward be.

*He that is weak.* He is weak who distinguishes foods, thinking some clean, others unclean, because the Jews were forbidden to eat; and he says this man is to be left to his own judgment, lest he eat with scruple. Or, although the faith be perfect which believes all things lawful, yet let the weak man, prone to a fall, who is easily laid low by the assault of lust, eat herbs, that is, thin and dry foods, which are not the fuel of vices, and let him abstain from those things by which lust is stirred up. For the richness of flesh-meats and delicious feasts provoke the body to lust.

*He that eateth.* Above he enjoined that we should not dispute about the thoughts of others, here he enjoins that we should not despise them.

*Let him not judge. ((AUG., lib. II de Ser. Dom. in monte.))* Judgment is to be made of manifest things, not of hidden things, etc., *as far as* whatsoever human foods indifferently to be taken.

*To his own Lord he standeth.* Concerning the unknown heart of another's servant thou hast not to judge, but his own Lord, to whose honor he that stands, stands; to whom belongs also the fall of him that falls, who can raise up or judge. *He standeth, or falleth,* he therefore says: because it is ambiguous; perhaps he stands who is thought to fall. *He standeth or falleth.* By this he shows that he does not know with what mind that man conducts himself in doubtful matters. *But he shall stand.* Here he intimates that ambiguous things we ought to turn to the better part, and to wish rather the safety than the death of the accused, and to have hope of good in the future, even if it be otherwise in the present. *But he shall stand.* Because neither if he eats is he guilty, nor if he does not eat, provided he does this out of devotion.

*For one.* Above he said that some eat all things, others not all; and speaking of the kinds of foods he says this, that some abstain at every time, others at some certain time, and he says that either may rightly be done. *In his own sense.* That is, let him be left to his own judgment, lest, having suffered scandal, he withdraw from charity, which is the mother of all virtues.

*He that regardeth.* *In his own sense* I say, as one abounding: because he that regardeth a day, whether every day, or a day interposed, regardeth it unto the Lord. *And he that eateth, eateth unto the Lord.* That is, unto the honor of the Lord, whose created things he believes to be all clean, and because, being about to serve him, he is sustained by them.

*For none of us liveth to himself.* For he who is bridled by the law lives not to himself, but to God, who gave the law. If there were no law, each man would live to himself. *To himself.* But unto the Lord, by whose judgment he is damned or crowned; or, *to himself*, that is, unto his own praise, but unto God's. For as of his greatness there is no end, so of our praise there will be no end. For when we shall have died in this flesh, we shall not cease to praise God. And according to this he treats of the faithful only. *Or to himself*, that is, to be judged by himself, but by the Lord: according to this it is taken of both the good and the evil.

*Before the tribunal.* This is said from a likeness: for the tribunal is the seat of the judge, which is placed on high, that the judge may be seen by all and himself from the eminent place may be able to behold all. So also Christ will sit as it were on a tribunal, because he will be seen by all, and he himself will see the consciences of all, and will judge their causes.

notes.text: Till seventy times seven — That is, as often as there is occasion. A certain number is put for an uncertain.
Therefore — In this respect.

One was brought who owed him ten thousand talents — According to the usual computation, if these were talents of gold, this would amount to seventy-two millions sterling. If they were talents of silver, it must have been four millions, four hundred thousand pounds. Hereby our Lord intimates the vast number and weight of our offenses against God, and our utter incapacity of making him any satisfaction.
As he had not to pay, his Lord commanded him to be sold — Such was the power which creditors anciently had over their insolvent debtors in several countries.
Went with him before a magistrate, and cast him into prison, protesting he should lie there, till he should pay the whole debt.

glossa.text: *Therefore is likened.* That you may know that one must forgive one's fellow servants, I will show by a likeness, that if that king and lord forgave his servant, much more must a man forgive his fellow servants.

*And his wife.* Him, not only the people, but also the prelates and the subjects, together with all their household or substance, he delivered over to foreign nations for the greatness of their offences: that what they would not pay by vow, they might pay by torment. He commanded them to pay the penalties for their covetousness and their works, as for a wife and children.

*And moved with pity.* The merciful Lord not only loosed the Jewish captivity, but also promised that at the coming of Christ he would give pardon of all sins, if they persisted in what they had begun. *He forgave him.* That is, he loosed him from the weight of carnal observances, and forgave the debt, that is, his former transgressions.

*He found one.* The Gentile people he wearied, as though it were his debtor: saying that the grace of Christ was not unto salvation for them, not only by persuasions, but even by torments he exacted carnal observances from them.

*Thou wicked servant.* Often have I forgiven thee thy debts, when thou didst ask in thy straits; but being set free thou hadst no compassion, nay rather thou persecutest the prophets and the apostles, and, ungrateful and presuming upon justice, thou despisest the Gentiles, judging them unworthy of thy fellowship in Christ.

hymns.title: Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord
Glorious things of thee are spoken
Lonely the boat, sailing at sea
The Lord comes, the Lord comes
Many and great, O God, are thy things

echoes.text: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
echoes.note: Paul's explicit formula-citation in 14:11 ('it is written, As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee will bow, every tongue will confess to God') quotes Isaiah 45:23 LXX. In Isaiah the universal bowing and swearing/confessing is rendered to YHWH alone as the only God and Savior; Paul deploys it to ground the certainty of universal accountability at the divine judgment seat. The same verse recurs at Philippians 2:10-11, showing Pauline thematic recurrence.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: The clean/unclean food dispute underlying 14:1-12 (and explicit in 14:14,20, 'nothing is unclean of itself... all things indeed are clean') directly engages the Levitical purity code distinguishing clean from unclean animals (Leviticus 11; cf. Deuteronomy 14). The 'weak' likely keep these distinctions; Paul's verdict that nothing is koinon in itself overturns the categorical force of Leviticus 11 for those in Christ.

echoes.text: but in very deed, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with Yahweh’s glory;
echoes.note: The introductory divine-oath formula 'As I live, says the Lord' (zōn egō legei kyrios) prefixed to the Isaiah 45 quotation is not in Isaiah 45:23 itself; it is the LXX oath formula 'as I live' (ζῶ ἐγώ) characteristic of Numbers 14:21,28 and Ezekiel. Paul (or his Vorlage) conflates the oath formula with the Isaiah quotation to heighten its solemnity as a guarantee of universal judgment.

echoes.text: Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green herb, I have given everything to you.
echoes.note: The position that 'one has faith to eat all things' (panta phagein, 14:2) echoes the post-flood Noahic grant: 'Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you; as the green plants I gave you everything' (Genesis 9:3). Paul's 'all things are clean' (14:14,20) presupposes this universal grant of food over against later dietary restriction.

echoes.text: You shall not eat any abominable thing. These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the chamois. Every animal that parts the hoof, and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, that may you eat. Nevertheless these you shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of those who have the hoof cloven: the camel, the hare, and the […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's parallel dietary legislation ('You shall not eat any abominable thing') reinforces the Levitical clean/unclean backdrop to the eating dispute. The 'weak in faith' who eat only vegetables may be observing scruples derived from this Torah food law (and/or avoiding marketplace meat of uncertain provenance).

echoes.text: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself. Now God made Daniel to find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs. The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse […]
echoes.note: Daniel and his companions refuse the king's rich food and wine, eating only vegetables (LXX lachana / ospria) and water to avoid defilement (Daniel 1:12,16). This is the closest Scriptural antecedent to a diaspora Jew eating 'only vegetables' (14:2) out of purity scruple in a Gentile environment, providing a likely model for the 'weak.'

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes all around, and see: all these gather themselves together, and come to you. As I live,” says Yahweh, “you shall surely clothe yourself with them all as with an ornament, and dress yourself with them, like a bride.
echoes.note: An alternative/complementary source for the prefixed oath 'As I live, says the Lord': Isaiah 49:18 ('As I live, says the LORD') stands within the same section of Isaiah as 45:23, making it a plausible internal-Isaianic source for the conflated formula rather than the Numbers/Ezekiel oath stock.

echoes.text: Therefore as I live, says the Lord Yahweh, surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things, and with all your abominations, therefore will I also diminish you; neither shall my eye spare, and I also will have no pity.
echoes.note: Ezekiel is the densest concentration of the 'As I live, says the Lord' oath (Ezekiel 5:11; 14:16; 16:48; 33:11, etc.). The recurrence of the formula there may stand behind the LXX phrasing Paul attaches to the Isaiah citation; faint and not pointed to a single verse.

echoes.text: God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.
echoes.note: The 'weak' eating only vegetables (lachana, 14:2) recalls the original Edenic vegetarian diet granted to humanity (Genesis 1:29, every seed-bearing plant for food). The contrast of vegetable-only vs. eating-all-things may evoke the pre-Noahic dietary order; thematic and faint, not verbal.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: Paul's axiom 'none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself... we are the Lord's' (14:7-8) reflects the creational logic that life is a gift wholly owed to its Giver (cf. Genesis 2:7, the breath of life from God). Faint thematic resonance of creaturely belonging rather than verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.
echoes.note: 'We are the Lord's' (tou kyriou esmen, 14:8) echoes the creational ownership confessed in Psalm 24:1 ('The earth is the LORD's and its fullness'), which Paul cites elsewhere at 1 Corinthians 10:26 in a closely parallel food-and-conscience argument. The lordship grounding here is conceptually linked though not quoted.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: 'Each one of us will give account of himself to God' (14:12) coheres with the Wisdom expectation that 'God will bring every deed into judgment' (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Thematic accountability before the divine Judge; faint and conceptual.

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: The motif of individual rendering of account to God who judges (14:10,12) resonates with Psalm 62:12 ('you will render to each according to his work'), a verse Paul invokes for judgment-according-to-works at Romans 2:6. The shared judgment-recompense logic links the chapters.

echoes.text: Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?
echoes.note: 'We will all stand before the judgment seat of God/Christ' (14:10) carries the prophetic Day-of-the-LORD note of standing before the dread Judge (cf. Joel 2:11, 'who can endure it?'), reframed by Paul christologically. Very faint thematic echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”
echoes.note: 'Until seventy times seven' (or 'seventy-seven') deliberately reverses Lamech's boast 'If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold': the same numbers that measured escalating vengeance now measure limitless forgiveness. The LXX of Gen 4:24 reads hebdomekontakis hepta, matching Jesus' phrasing.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: “For three transgressions of Damascus, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron;
echoes.note: Peter's 'seven times' as a presumed limit may echo the prophetic 'for three transgressions and for four' idiom of a fixed tally of offenses before judgment; Jesus dissolves the tally. Faint formal parallel.

echoes.text: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins? He being himself flesh nourishes wrath: Who will make atonement for his sins? Remember your […]
echoes.note: The parable's logic — God forgives the one who forgives, and withholds mercy from the unmerciful — is the narrative form of Sirach's teaching: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray... Does anyone harbor anger against another, and expect healing from the Lord?' The closest extracanonical parallel to the whole pericope.

echoes.text: At the end of every seven years, you shall cancel debts. This is the way it shall be done: every creditor shall release that which he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not require payment from his neighbor and his brother; because Yahweh’s release has been proclaimed.
echoes.note: The king who 'releases' (aphiemi) his servant and 'forgives the debt' enacts the sabbatical-year release of debts (shemittah): every creditor shall release what he has lent. The unforgiving servant violates the release he himself received.

echoes.text: “‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave.
echoes.note: The command to sell the debtor 'with his wife and children' reflects the legal reality of debt-slavery regulated in the Jubilee laws ('if your brother becomes poor and sells himself to you'), the very bondage the king's compassion suspends.

echoes.text: Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets to Elisha, saying, “Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared Yahweh. Now the creditor has come to take for himself my two children to be slaves.”
echoes.note: A creditor coming to seize the debtor's children as slaves (the widow's plea to Elisha) supplies the social backdrop for selling the man 'with his wife, his children, and all that he had.'

echoes.text: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
echoes.note: 'Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered' is the proverbial kernel of the parable: the servant who refuses his fellow's plea forfeits the mercy he had begged and received.

echoes.text: Yet now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children as their children. Behold, we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters have been brought into bondage. Neither is it in our power to help it; for other men have our fields and our vineyards.”
echoes.note: The outcry that 'we are forcing our sons and daughters to be slaves' to pay debts parallels the parable's seizure of family for an unpayable obligation. Contributory social context.

echoes.text: Whoever mocks the poor reproaches his Maker. He who is glad at calamity shall not be unpunished.
echoes.note: 'He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker; he who is glad at calamity shall not go unpunished' supports the measure-for-measure judgment on the merciless servant. Faint.

echoes.text: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; if there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.
echoes.note: Daniel's counsel to the king to 'break off your sins by showing mercy to the oppressed' links royal forgiveness with the showing of mercy demanded of the forgiven — a possible backdrop to the king/mercy frame. Contested.

notes.text: Joseph will peradventure hate us — While their father lived, they thought themselves safe under his shadow; but now he was dead, they feared the worst. A guilty conscience exposeth men to continual frights; those that would be fearless must keep themselves guiltless.
Thy father did command — Thus in humbling ourselves to Christ by faith and repentance, we may plead that it is the command of his father and our father we should do so.

We are the servants of the God of thy father — Not only children of the same Jacob, but worshippers of the same Jehovah. Though we must be ready to forgive all that injure us, yet we must especially take heed of bearing malice towards any that are the servants of the God of our father; those we should always treat with a peculiar tenderness, for we and they have the same master. He wept when they spake to him - These were tears of sorrow for their suspicion of him, and tears of tenderness upon their submission.

Am I in the place of God? — He in his great humility thought they shewed him too much respect, and faith to them in effect, as Peter to Cornelius, Stand up, I myself also am a man. Make your peace with God, and then you will find it an easy matter to make your peace with me.
Ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good — In order to the making Joseph a greater blessing to his family than otherwise he could have been.

Fear not, I will nourish you — See what an excellent spirit Joseph was of, and learn of him to render good for evil. He did not tell them they were upon their good behaviour, and he would be kind to them if he saw they carried themselves well: no, he would not thus hold them in suspence, nor seem jealous of them, though they had been suspicious of him. He comforted them, and, to banish all their fears, he spake kindly to them. Those we love and forgive we must not only do well for, but speak kindly to.

glossa.text: « And when the time of the mourning was expired, » etc. ((AUG.)) As to what Joseph enjoined upon the great men of Egypt, that they should say to Pharao in his name: « My father made me swear, saying: In the monument which I made for myself in the land of Chanaan, there thou shalt bury me; » it is asked how this may be true, since these words of his father, when he gave charge concerning his burial, are not read. But the words are to be referred to the sense, as other things above were likewise repeated. For words must serve a will that is to be uttered and brought to knowledge. But that Jacob dug himself a sepulchre is nowhere read above, yet assuredly, unless he had dug it, it would not now be said.

notes.text: The eagles — Which lives long in great strength and vigour.
So great — So much above their deserts and expectations.

glossa.text: *Bless, O soul.* ((AUG.)) After the prayers of the poor man, the proclamations of one rejoicing. All who are in Christ are as it were one man, who rouses and exhorts his own soul to bless the Lord, wishing to define why he is to be blessed, lest any be found slothful thereto. Cry with the voice, if there is a man who *qut* hears; without voice, if there is no man to hear, because God hears. ((CASS.)) By his own benefits he exhorts men to bless God. ((AUG.)) The prophet, speaking in the person of the just man in general, according to the higher power of the soul, that is, the reason, exhorts the soul to bless, saying: *Forget not.* Let not the delight of sin be before thine eyes, but the condemnation and the remission of God: think over all thine evils, because as many as they are, so many are the good retributions of God. *Retributions.* Not bestowings. Man bestows evils for goods, and God requites him with goods for evils. He bestowed when he made me, he requites when he justifies.

*Who forgiveth.* ((AUG.)) This he does in the sacrament of baptism. *Who healeth all thy diseases.* This he does in the life of a faithful man, while the flesh lusts against the spirit, so that we do such things as we would not; and those languors of the old state are healed from day to day, as newness increases, out of the faith which works through love.

*Who redeemeth thy life from corruption.* This is done in the last resurrection of the dead. *Who crowneth,* etc. This is done at the judgment, where, when the king shall sit upon his throne, about to render to every man according to his works , who shall boast that he has a heart glorious and clean from sin? Therefore it was necessary to make mention of mercy and of compassions in that place where dues would seem to be so rendered that there should be no room left for mercy.
*Thy youth like the eagle's.* ((AUG.)) So great a likeness is set down, etc., *as far as* whose mouth old age has closed, who have forgotten to eat our bread.

*He that doeth.* ((AUG.)) The second part, where he admonishes men to bless like *par*; read *per*, "through" those things which were done for the men of old, and are done for those that come after. *Mercies.* Which they shall obtain who love their enemies, etc., *as far as* for after *mercy* he adds concerning judgment, saying, *And judgment.*
*To Moses.* ((AUG.)) By Moses, all the saints, etc., *as far as* through whom he gave the law, that the beloved *dilectum*; read *delictum*, "the offence" might abound.

*For.* ((ID.)) The heaven is on every side about the earth, whence there is even for them that sin light, air, breath, rain, whence fruit: without heaven the earth comes to an end, so is the protection of God over them that fear him.

*How far distant,* etc. ((ID.)) When sin is forgiven, sins set, grace rises, sins are in their setting; turn thyself away, therefore, from the setting of sins, and stretch toward the rising of grace, and thou risest.

notes.text: Him that is weak — Through needless scruples. Receive - With all love and courtesy into Christian fellowship. But not to doubtful disputations - About questionable points.
All things — All sorts of food, though forbidden by the law.

Despise him that eateth not — As over-scrupulous or superstitious. Judge him that eateth - As profane, or taking undue liberties. For God hath received him - Into the number of his children, notwithstanding this.
One day above another — As new moons, and other Jewish festivals. Let every man be fully persuaded - That a thing is lawful, before he does it.

Regardeth it to the Lord — That is, out of a principle of conscience toward God. To the Lord he doth not regard it - He also acts from a principle of conscience. He that eateth not - Flesh. Giveth God thanks - For his herbs.
None of us — Christians, in the things we do. Liveth to himself - Is at his own disposal; doeth his own will.
Or why dost thou despise thy brother — Hitherto the apostle as addressed the weak brother: now he speaks to the stronger.

As I live — An oath proper to him, because he only possesseth life infinite and independent. It is Christ who is here termed both Lord and God; as it is he to whom we live, and to whom we die. Every tongue shall confess to God - Shall own him as their rightful Lord; which shall then only be accomplished in its full extent. The Lord grant we may find mercy in that day; and may it also be imparted to those who have differed from us! yea, to those who have censured and condemned us for things which we have done from a desire to please him, or refused to do from a fear of offending him. Isaiah xlv, 23

glossa.text: *Now him that is weak.* It belongs to a perfect faith to distinguish no food, nor to think it unclean, because *all things are clean to the clean.* But certain weak ones judged that some things were to be abstained from, and so there was contention among the Romans; whence he enjoins that such be taken up, not cast off, but by bearing with them, by example and by word, to be raised up to faith. And if it is unknown with what mind anyone does a thing, not to dispute about it. *Not in disputes.* He is not to be condemned whose thought is not open, or of whom we know not what sort he will afterward be.

*He that is weak.* He is weak who distinguishes foods, thinking some clean, others unclean, because the Jews were forbidden to eat; and he says this man is to be left to his own judgment, lest he eat with scruple. Or, although the faith be perfect which believes all things lawful, yet let the weak man, prone to a fall, who is easily laid low by the assault of lust, eat herbs, that is, thin and dry foods, which are not the fuel of vices, and let him abstain from those things by which lust is stirred up. For the richness of flesh-meats and delicious feasts provoke the body to lust.

*He that eateth.* Above he enjoined that we should not dispute about the thoughts of others, here he enjoins that we should not despise them.

*Let him not judge. ((AUG., lib. II de Ser. Dom. in monte.))* Judgment is to be made of manifest things, not of hidden things, etc., *as far as* whatsoever human foods indifferently to be taken.

*To his own Lord he standeth.* Concerning the unknown heart of another's servant thou hast not to judge, but his own Lord, to whose honor he that stands, stands; to whom belongs also the fall of him that falls, who can raise up or judge. *He standeth, or falleth,* he therefore says: because it is ambiguous; perhaps he stands who is thought to fall. *He standeth or falleth.* By this he shows that he does not know with what mind that man conducts himself in doubtful matters. *But he shall stand.* Here he intimates that ambiguous things we ought to turn to the better part, and to wish rather the safety than the death of the accused, and to have hope of good in the future, even if it be otherwise in the present. *But he shall stand.* Because neither if he eats is he guilty, nor if he does not eat, provided he does this out of devotion.

*For one.* Above he said that some eat all things, others not all; and speaking of the kinds of foods he says this, that some abstain at every time, others at some certain time, and he says that either may rightly be done. *In his own sense.* That is, let him be left to his own judgment, lest, having suffered scandal, he withdraw from charity, which is the mother of all virtues.

*He that regardeth.* *In his own sense* I say, as one abounding: because he that regardeth a day, whether every day, or a day interposed, regardeth it unto the Lord. *And he that eateth, eateth unto the Lord.* That is, unto the honor of the Lord, whose created things he believes to be all clean, and because, being about to serve him, he is sustained by them.

*For none of us liveth to himself.* For he who is bridled by the law lives not to himself, but to God, who gave the law. If there were no law, each man would live to himself. *To himself.* But unto the Lord, by whose judgment he is damned or crowned; or, *to himself*, that is, unto his own praise, but unto God's. For as of his greatness there is no end, so of our praise there will be no end. For when we shall have died in this flesh, we shall not cease to praise God. And according to this he treats of the faithful only. *Or to himself*, that is, to be judged by himself, but by the Lord: according to this it is taken of both the good and the evil.

*Before the tribunal.* This is said from a likeness: for the tribunal is the seat of the judge, which is placed on high, that the judge may be seen by all and himself from the eminent place may be able to behold all. So also Christ will sit as it were on a tribunal, because he will be seen by all, and he himself will see the consciences of all, and will judge their causes.

notes.text: Till seventy times seven — That is, as often as there is occasion. A certain number is put for an uncertain.
Therefore — In this respect.

One was brought who owed him ten thousand talents — According to the usual computation, if these were talents of gold, this would amount to seventy-two millions sterling. If they were talents of silver, it must have been four millions, four hundred thousand pounds. Hereby our Lord intimates the vast number and weight of our offenses against God, and our utter incapacity of making him any satisfaction.
As he had not to pay, his Lord commanded him to be sold — Such was the power which creditors anciently had over their insolvent debtors in several countries.
Went with him before a magistrate, and cast him into prison, protesting he should lie there, till he should pay the whole debt.

glossa.text: *Therefore is likened.* That you may know that one must forgive one's fellow servants, I will show by a likeness, that if that king and lord forgave his servant, much more must a man forgive his fellow servants.

*And his wife.* Him, not only the people, but also the prelates and the subjects, together with all their household or substance, he delivered over to foreign nations for the greatness of their offences: that what they would not pay by vow, they might pay by torment. He commanded them to pay the penalties for their covetousness and their works, as for a wife and children.

*And moved with pity.* The merciful Lord not only loosed the Jewish captivity, but also promised that at the coming of Christ he would give pardon of all sins, if they persisted in what they had begun. *He forgave him.* That is, he loosed him from the weight of carnal observances, and forgave the debt, that is, his former transgressions.

*He found one.* The Gentile people he wearied, as though it were his debtor: saying that the grace of Christ was not unto salvation for them, not only by persuasions, but even by torments he exacted carnal observances from them.

*Thou wicked servant.* Often have I forgiven thee thy debts, when thou didst ask in thy straits; but being set free thou hadst no compassion, nay rather thou persecutest the prophets and the apostles, and, ungrateful and presuming upon justice, thou despisest the Gentiles, judging them unworthy of thy fellowship in Christ.

Dear Jesus, as a hen covers her chicks
Christ loves the church, with grace beyond all measure

echoes.text: I have sworn by myself, the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and will not return, that to me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall take an oath.
echoes.note: Paul's explicit formula-citation in 14:11 ('it is written, As I live, says the Lord, to me every knee will bow, every tongue will confess to God') quotes Isaiah 45:23 LXX. In Isaiah the universal bowing and swearing/confessing is rendered to YHWH alone as the only God and Savior; Paul deploys it to ground the certainty of universal accountability at the divine judgment seat. The same verse recurs at Philippians 2:10-11, showing Pauline thematic recurrence.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them, “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘These are the living things which you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat. “‘Nevertheless these you shall not eat of those that chew the cud, or of those who part the hoof: the camel, because he chews the cud but doesn’t have a parted hoof, he is […]
echoes.note: The clean/unclean food dispute underlying 14:1-12 (and explicit in 14:14,20, 'nothing is unclean of itself... all things indeed are clean') directly engages the Levitical purity code distinguishing clean from unclean animals (Leviticus 11; cf. Deuteronomy 14). The 'weak' likely keep these distinctions; Paul's verdict that nothing is koinon in itself overturns the categorical force of Leviticus 11 for those in Christ.

echoes.text: but in very deed, as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with Yahweh’s glory;
echoes.note: The introductory divine-oath formula 'As I live, says the Lord' (zōn egō legei kyrios) prefixed to the Isaiah 45 quotation is not in Isaiah 45:23 itself; it is the LXX oath formula 'as I live' (ζῶ ἐγώ) characteristic of Numbers 14:21,28 and Ezekiel. Paul (or his Vorlage) conflates the oath formula with the Isaiah quotation to heighten its solemnity as a guarantee of universal judgment.

echoes.text: Every moving thing that lives will be food for you. As I gave you the green herb, I have given everything to you.
echoes.note: The position that 'one has faith to eat all things' (panta phagein, 14:2) echoes the post-flood Noahic grant: 'Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you; as the green plants I gave you everything' (Genesis 9:3). Paul's 'all things are clean' (14:14,20) presupposes this universal grant of food over against later dietary restriction.

echoes.text: You shall not eat any abominable thing. These are the animals which you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the roebuck, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope, and the chamois. Every animal that parts the hoof, and has the hoof cloven in two and chews the cud, among the animals, that may you eat. Nevertheless these you shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of those who have the hoof cloven: the camel, the hare, and the […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's parallel dietary legislation ('You shall not eat any abominable thing') reinforces the Levitical clean/unclean backdrop to the eating dispute. The 'weak in faith' who eat only vegetables may be observing scruples derived from this Torah food law (and/or avoiding marketplace meat of uncertain provenance).

echoes.text: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself. Now God made Daniel to find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs. The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse […]
echoes.note: Daniel and his companions refuse the king's rich food and wine, eating only vegetables (LXX lachana / ospria) and water to avoid defilement (Daniel 1:12,16). This is the closest Scriptural antecedent to a diaspora Jew eating 'only vegetables' (14:2) out of purity scruple in a Gentile environment, providing a likely model for the 'weak.'

echoes.text: Lift up your eyes all around, and see: all these gather themselves together, and come to you. As I live,” says Yahweh, “you shall surely clothe yourself with them all as with an ornament, and dress yourself with them, like a bride.
echoes.note: An alternative/complementary source for the prefixed oath 'As I live, says the Lord': Isaiah 49:18 ('As I live, says the LORD') stands within the same section of Isaiah as 45:23, making it a plausible internal-Isaianic source for the conflated formula rather than the Numbers/Ezekiel oath stock.

echoes.text: Therefore as I live, says the Lord Yahweh, surely, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things, and with all your abominations, therefore will I also diminish you; neither shall my eye spare, and I also will have no pity.
echoes.note: Ezekiel is the densest concentration of the 'As I live, says the Lord' oath (Ezekiel 5:11; 14:16; 16:48; 33:11, etc.). The recurrence of the formula there may stand behind the LXX phrasing Paul attaches to the Isaiah citation; faint and not pointed to a single verse.

echoes.text: God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.
echoes.note: The 'weak' eating only vegetables (lachana, 14:2) recalls the original Edenic vegetarian diet granted to humanity (Genesis 1:29, every seed-bearing plant for food). The contrast of vegetable-only vs. eating-all-things may evoke the pre-Noahic dietary order; thematic and faint, not verbal.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: Paul's axiom 'none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself... we are the Lord's' (14:7-8) reflects the creational logic that life is a gift wholly owed to its Giver (cf. Genesis 2:7, the breath of life from God). Faint thematic resonance of creaturely belonging rather than verbal borrowing.

echoes.text: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell therein.
echoes.note: 'We are the Lord's' (tou kyriou esmen, 14:8) echoes the creational ownership confessed in Psalm 24:1 ('The earth is the LORD's and its fullness'), which Paul cites elsewhere at 1 Corinthians 10:26 in a closely parallel food-and-conscience argument. The lordship grounding here is conceptually linked though not quoted.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: 'Each one of us will give account of himself to God' (14:12) coheres with the Wisdom expectation that 'God will bring every deed into judgment' (Ecclesiastes 12:14). Thematic accountability before the divine Judge; faint and conceptual.

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: The motif of individual rendering of account to God who judges (14:10,12) resonates with Psalm 62:12 ('you will render to each according to his work'), a verse Paul invokes for judgment-according-to-works at Romans 2:6. The shared judgment-recompense logic links the chapters.

echoes.text: Yahweh thunders his voice before his army; for his forces are very great; for he is strong who obeys his command; for the day of Yahweh is great and very awesome, and who can endure it?
echoes.note: 'We will all stand before the judgment seat of God/Christ' (14:10) carries the prophetic Day-of-the-LORD note of standing before the dread Judge (cf. Joel 2:11, 'who can endure it?'), reframed by Paul christologically. Very faint thematic echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”
echoes.note: 'Until seventy times seven' (or 'seventy-seven') deliberately reverses Lamech's boast 'If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold': the same numbers that measured escalating vengeance now measure limitless forgiveness. The LXX of Gen 4:24 reads hebdomekontakis hepta, matching Jesus' phrasing.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh: “For three transgressions of Damascus, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron;
echoes.note: Peter's 'seven times' as a presumed limit may echo the prophetic 'for three transgressions and for four' idiom of a fixed tally of offenses before judgment; Jesus dissolves the tally. Faint formal parallel.

echoes.text: He that takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord; And he will surely make firm his sins. Forgive your neighbor the hurt that he has done you; And then your sins will be pardoned when you pray. Man cherisheth anger against man; And does he seek healing from the Lord? Upon a man like himself he has no mercy; And does he make supplication for his own sins? He being himself flesh nourishes wrath: Who will make atonement for his sins? Remember your […]
echoes.note: The parable's logic — God forgives the one who forgives, and withholds mercy from the unmerciful — is the narrative form of Sirach's teaching: 'Forgive your neighbor the wrong he has done, and then your sins will be pardoned when you pray... Does anyone harbor anger against another, and expect healing from the Lord?' The closest extracanonical parallel to the whole pericope.

echoes.text: At the end of every seven years, you shall cancel debts. This is the way it shall be done: every creditor shall release that which he has lent to his neighbor. He shall not require payment from his neighbor and his brother; because Yahweh’s release has been proclaimed.
echoes.note: The king who 'releases' (aphiemi) his servant and 'forgives the debt' enacts the sabbatical-year release of debts (shemittah): every creditor shall release what he has lent. The unforgiving servant violates the release he himself received.

echoes.text: “‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave.
echoes.note: The command to sell the debtor 'with his wife and children' reflects the legal reality of debt-slavery regulated in the Jubilee laws ('if your brother becomes poor and sells himself to you'), the very bondage the king's compassion suspends.

echoes.text: Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets to Elisha, saying, “Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared Yahweh. Now the creditor has come to take for himself my two children to be slaves.”
echoes.note: A creditor coming to seize the debtor's children as slaves (the widow's plea to Elisha) supplies the social backdrop for selling the man 'with his wife, his children, and all that he had.'

echoes.text: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
echoes.note: 'Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be answered' is the proverbial kernel of the parable: the servant who refuses his fellow's plea forfeits the mercy he had begged and received.

echoes.text: Yet now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children as their children. Behold, we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters have been brought into bondage. Neither is it in our power to help it; for other men have our fields and our vineyards.”
echoes.note: The outcry that 'we are forcing our sons and daughters to be slaves' to pay debts parallels the parable's seizure of family for an unpayable obligation. Contributory social context.

echoes.text: Whoever mocks the poor reproaches his Maker. He who is glad at calamity shall not be unpunished.
echoes.note: 'He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker; he who is glad at calamity shall not go unpunished' supports the measure-for-measure judgment on the merciless servant. Faint.

echoes.text: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you, and break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; if there may be a lengthening of your tranquility.
echoes.note: Daniel's counsel to the king to 'break off your sins by showing mercy to the oppressed' links royal forgiveness with the showing of mercy demanded of the forgiven — a possible backdrop to the king/mercy frame. Contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: How often should I forgive? Seventy times seven.
As far as the east is from the west, God removes our sin.
You meant it for evil; God meant it for good.
The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger.
We have been forgiven a debt we could never pay.
Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not his mercy.
Come, let us worship the God of second chances.
We come, forgiven, to forgive. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture the whole earth between the sunrise and the sunset, the farthest east from the farthest west — that is the distance God has carried your sin away.
So far does God remove our sin.
We come carrying old debts and longer grudges, the ledgers we keep on one another.
So far does God remove our sin.
The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, and does not deal with us as we deserve.
So far does God remove our sin.
What others meant for harm, God has woven toward good; what we owed, the King has wiped clean.
So far does God remove our sin.
So loose the grudge, forgive the debt, and come and bless the Lord.
So far does God remove our sin. Bless the Lord, O my soul!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: How many times must I forgive? More than I can count.
As far as east is from west, God carries our sin away.
We come with old debts and longer grudges.
As far as east is from west, God carries our sin away.
The Lord is merciful and slow to anger.
As far as east is from west, God carries our sin away.
Come, let us bless the God who forgives.
We come, forgiven, to forgive. Amen.

turn.trap: Becomes either a demand for infinite tolerance of ongoing harm (weaponized against those still being hurt) or pure quibbling over "seventy times seven" as a literal count — missing that the parable's turn is the comparison, not the number: ten thousand talents against a hundred denarii.
turn.hinge: The king doesn't merely cancel the debt — he has genuine compassion first, and the servant still can't extend an ounce of it downward. Receiving mercy and extending it are supposed to be the same reflex; the parable is about the gap when they aren't.

doors.claim: The king's mercy exceeds the servant's request — he asked only for patience, and received the whole debt cancelled.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: See the exuberance of heavenly love! The servant asked only a brief respite, but he gives him more than he had asked, a full remittance and cancelling of the whole debt.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: This command issued not of cruelty, but of unspeakable tenderness. For he seeks by these terrors to bring him to plead that he be not sold.

doors.say: You never have to negotiate God down to what you think you deserve — he cancels more than you had the nerve to ask for.
doors.do: Have them name one thing they've been asking God for a mere delay on, when the actual offer on the table is full cancellation.

doors.claim: The incommensurable gap between what he owed and what was owed to him is the whole point — sins against us are real, but never remotely to that scale.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: There is as great difference between sins committed against men, and sins committed against God, as between ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: The ten thousand talents which he owed denote all sins which can be done under the Law.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Hereby our Lord intimates the vast number and weight of our offenses against God, and our utter incapacity of making him any satisfaction.

doors.say: Whatever's owed to you is real — but do the math the parable does before you decide it's unforgivable.
doors.do: Ask them to put a number, even a made-up one, on what they were forgiven versus what they're refusing to forgive.

doors.claim: The servant abused his fellow the instant he left the king's presence — forgiveness received doesn't survive contact with reality unless it's extended immediately, not stored up.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: By saying, 'as he went out,' He shews that it was not after long time, but immediately; while the favour he had received still sounded in his ears, he abused it.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: He therefore, as I suppose, took him by the throat, because he had come forth from the king.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Often have I forgiven thee thy debts, when thou didst ask in thy straits; but being set free thou hadst no compassion.

doors.say: The mercy you just received doesn't automatically travel with you out the door — it has to be carried on purpose.
doors.do: Ask them to identify the last time they received grace and then, within the hour, withheld it from someone else.

doors.landing: Am I in the place of God?
doors.claim: Joseph has the power to repay and refuses it: judgment belongs to God, who was working good through the very evil done to him.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Am I in the place of God? — He in his great humility thought they shewed him too much respect. Make your peace with God, and then you will find it an easy matter to make your peace with me.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good — in order to the making Joseph a greater blessing to his family than otherwise he could have been.

doors.say: Joseph could have had his revenge. Instead he asked: who am I to sit in God's chair?
doors.do: Ask them to name the person they have been quietly judging, and to hand that judgment back to God in prayer.

doors.claim: Joseph's forgiveness comes without probation: he does not keep his brothers on good behavior but comforts them and speaks kindly.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: He did not tell them they were upon their good behaviour, and he would be kind to them if he saw they carried themselves well. He comforted them, and spake kindly to them. Those we love and forgive we must not only do well for, but speak kindly to.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: While their father lived, they thought themselves safe under his shadow; but now he was dead, they feared the worst. A guilty conscience exposeth men to continual frights.

doors.say: Forgiveness that keeps someone on probation isn't finished yet. Joseph didn't just forgive; he spoke kindly.
doors.do: Invite them to say one kind, unconditional word this week to someone they have forgiven but kept at arm's length.

complementary.gravity: With Jacob dead, the brothers fear Joseph will finally repay them, and Joseph weeps and answers, "Am I in the place of God? Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Genesis 50); the Psalm removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west; Paul asks, "Why dost thou judge thy brother?" (Romans 14); and Jesus tells of a servant forgiven a fortune who will not forgive a few coins. The nerve: forgiveness is not ours to ration, because judgment is not ours to hold.

synthesis.convergence: Joseph refuses to take God's place and repay his brothers (Genesis 50); the Psalm pictures sin removed as far as east from west (Psalm 103); Paul reminds the Romans that each stands before God, not before one another (Romans 14); and the servant forgiven everything seizes a fellow over a little (Matthew 18). Each reading hands judgment back to God, and in the space the grudge leaves, forgiveness becomes possible.
synthesis.claim: You are not in the place of God: let the debt go, because the one who could collect it has already forgiven you.
synthesis.here: For people keeping a quiet ledger of old wrongs, especially in families, the move is Joseph's question — am I in the place of God? — asked honestly, before trying to feel forgiving.

semicontinuous.gravity: Israel walks through the sea on dry ground while Egypt drowns behind them (Exodus 14); Paul insists none of us lives to ourselves, so stop judging one another (Romans 14); and Peter's careful math — "how many times, seven?" — gets answered with a number that isn't really a number, and a story about a debt too large to ever repay. The nerve: forgiveness stops being arithmetic the instant you remember the size of what you were already forgiven.

synthesis.convergence: Israel crosses on dry ground while their pursuers drown — an entire debt of slavery cancelled in one act they didn't earn (Exodus 14); Paul tells the Romans to stop judging each other because none of them lives to himself, they belong to the Lord who is judge enough (Romans 14); and the servant who's just had ten thousand talents forgiven can't forgive a hundred denarii. Every reading names the same gap: mercy received and mercy extended are supposed to be one gesture, and somehow never are without a fight.
synthesis.claim: You have already been forgiven a debt you could not have paid — the only question left is whether that memory survives you leaving the room.
synthesis.here: For people keeping score against someone who's wronged them far less than they've been forgiven, don't ask them to forgive on principle — ask them to do the math the parable does: ten thousand against a hundred.

turn.subtract: Three landings — mercy that exceeds the ask, the incommensurable debts, or how fast forgiveness curdled once he left the room. Choose one.
